content:
Hello!

I've an LLM researcher who has recently become interested in auto-formalization. My background is more in training/evals, and not so much in pure mathematics.

Like many people, it seemed to me with the rise of vibe coding, a language like Lean would become ideal. The provable correctness would allow LLMs many attempts at being "right" in an auditable way. I checked out the mathlib PRs to see if that held water, and was surprised to find that wasn't the case. Many AI PRs were outright rejected, not because they were _wrong_ but because they weren't useful. Mathlib has other goals outside of correctness, like generality, breaking parts of a proof down into composable parts that other people can use, etc. And these things were matters of taste.

Combine that with Many SWE Bench Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged last week, showing this was true of non-verifiable languages as well.

It seems to me that training purely off of verifiable rewards in RLVR cannot teach this taste. So it would be good if judges could be well-aligned with the taste of Mathlib reviewers. Then those could be used as reward models to create LLMs that could produce PRs aligned with Mathlibs goals.

To test this, I'm developing an evaluation called "ProofJudge". Here's how it works:

  1. I went through mathlib and selected ~100 PRs. I've pulled the base commit of that PR, the initial submitted version of the PR, and the final accepted version.
  2. An LLM judge agent is put in a docker container and shown the PR (either initial or final) applied to the base commit the PR came from. It does not know whether it is looking at the initial or final PR.
  3. It is asked to grade the PR from 1-7.
  4. We consider a judgement to be "correct" if the same model rates the final, approved PR (that is by definition more human agreeable) higher than the initial PR.

I've attached the rubric for grading that is being used, which came from looking at the PRs and Zulip chats. It is entirely possible I have missed some key elements of desirable PR properties. My plan is to submit this to AITP 2026 and publish it as an open-source evaluation. I would appreciate any suggestions on rubric the community has to offer. Thank you!
rubric.md

EDIT: I have a first draft of the results!

Just checking -- what do you do about people force pushing to PR branches? Presumably the initial state is not actually available there.

Similarly, do you try to treat the common situation where someone opens a very preliminary version of a PR marked as draft or WIP, and only later asks for review?
Perhaps these are simply not addressable, beyond noting them as a weaknesses in any report on this approach?

For the initial eval set, I did a lot of filtering. Currently there are only 100 pairs that have been pulled out as worth measuring.

I’m working on a better flow for parsing them automatically. The easiest thing thus far has just been to determine whether an llm judge finds the initial and final state that was extracted to be “significantly” different and then spot checking those manually.

I’d like to create a fuller dataset for training, but for the reasons you’ve listed it’ll be complicated to do. But definitely open to suggestions!
The paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.19110 did something similar based on commit history and have created the APEBench. Might be interesting for you @Shane Caldwell
It definitely is, thanks. Actually a very similar setup with a slightly different research question (similar enough I got nervous for a minute). I'll need to cite it for sure. Thanks Franz!

Early results here!

Most of the errors with GPT 5.4 (low reasoning) were actually just scoring the initial and final version of the PR with the same score. It seems very plausible to me that with a better rubric the ties would be breakable, and then we could move on to distilling this capability into a much smaller model (Qwen3 32b seems promising for that).
